options.why: Solved for $2\theta$ in $[0^{\circ}, 720^{\circ}]$ but forgot to divide each angle by $2$ to isolate $\theta$.
Solved for $u$ in $[0^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}]$ only, failing to transform the domain to $720^{\circ}$ and missing half the solutions.
Used reference angle $60^{\circ}$ instead of $30^{\circ}$ when evaluating $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.

questions.solution_text:
Let $u = 2\theta$, where $0^{\circ} \le u \le 720^{\circ}$.
$\cos u = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
Reference angle: $u_{\text{ref}} = 30^{\circ}$
$\cos u < 0$, so $u$ lies in Quadrants 2 and 3.
In $[0^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}]$: $u = 150^{\circ}, 210^{\circ}$
In $[360^{\circ}, 720^{\circ}]$: $u = 510^{\circ}, 570^{\circ}$
$2\theta = 150^{\circ}, 210^{\circ}, 510^{\circ}, 570^{\circ}$
$\theta = 75^{\circ}, 105^{\circ}, 255^{\circ}, 285^{\circ}$

options.why: Solved for the compound angle $2x$ in $[0, 4\pi]$ but forgot to divide by $2$ to obtain $x$.
Did not transform the domain to $4\pi$, finding only two solutions instead of four.
Used reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$ instead of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ for tangent ratio $\sqrt{3}$.

questions.solution_text:
Let $u = 2x$, where $0 \le u \le 4\pi$.
$\tan u = \sqrt{3}$
Reference angle: $u_{\text{ref}} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$
$\tan u > 0$, so $u$ lies in Quadrants 1 and 3.
In $[0, 2\pi]$: $u = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
In $[2\pi, 4\pi]$: $u = \dfrac{7\pi}{3}, \dfrac{10\pi}{3}$
$2x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}, \dfrac{7\pi}{3}, \dfrac{10\pi}{3}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$

options.why: Solved $\cos u = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ but forgot to back-substitute by adding $30^{\circ}$.
Found only the interior solution $x = 60^{\circ}$ and missed the boundary solutions $0^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$.
Subtracted $30^{circ}$ from $330^{circ}$ instead of adding $30^{circ}$ during back-substitution.

questions.solution_text:
Let $u = x - 30^{\circ}$, where $-30^{\circ} \le u \le 330^{\circ}$.
$\cos u = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
Reference angle: $u_{\text{ref}} = 30^{\circ}$
$\cos u > 0$, so $u$ lies in Quadrants 1 and 4.
In $[-30^{\circ}, 330^{\circ}]$: $u = -30^{\circ}, 30^{\circ}, 330^{\circ}$
$x - 30^{\circ} = -30^{\circ}, 30^{\circ}, 330^{\circ}$
$x = 0^{\circ}, 60^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}$

options.why: Solved $\sin u = -1$ to get $u = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ but forgot to back-substitute by adding $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
Subtracted $\frac{\pi}{2}$ from $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ instead of adding $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
Included solutions corresponding to $\sin u = 0$ as well as $\sin u = -1$.

questions.solution_text:
Let $u = x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le u \le \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
$\sin u = -1$
In $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$: $u = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$
$x - \dfrac{\pi}{2} = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$
$x = 0, 2\pi$

questions.solution_text:
Let $u = 2\theta - 30^{\circ}$, where $-30^{\circ} \le u < 690^{\circ}$.
$\tan u = 1$
Reference angle: $u_{\text{ref}} = 45^{\circ}$
$\tan u > 0$, so $u$ lies in Quadrants 1 and 3.
In $[-30^{\circ}, 690^{\circ}]$: $u = 45^{\circ}, 225^{\circ}, 405^{\circ}, 585^{\circ}$
$2\theta - 30^{\circ} = 45^{\circ}, 225^{\circ}, 405^{\circ}, 585^{\circ}$
$2\theta = 75^{\circ}, 255^{\circ}, 435^{\circ}, 615^{\circ}$
$\theta = 37.5^{\circ}, 127.5^{\circ}, 217.5^{\circ}, 307.5^{\circ}$

options.why: Solved for $\frac{\theta}{2} = 150^{\circ}$ but forgot to multiply by $2$ to find $\theta$.
Included the Quadrant 3 angle $u = 210^{\circ}$ which exceeds the transformed domain $[0^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}]$.
Solved for positive cosine $\cos u = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ in Quadrant 1 instead of negative cosine.

questions.solution_text:
Let $u = \dfrac{\theta}{2}$, where $0^{\circ} \le u \le 180^{\circ}$.
$\cos u = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
Reference angle: $u_{\text{ref}} = 30^{\circ}$
$\cos u < 0$, so $u$ is in Quadrant 2 in the domain $[0^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}]$.
$u = 180^{\circ} - 30^{\circ} = 150^{\circ}$
$\dfrac{\theta}{2} = 150^{\circ}$
$\theta = 300^{\circ}$

Solved for $u$ but forgot to subtract $\frac{\pi}{4}$ and divide by $2$ to isolate $x$.

questions.solution_text:
$2\cos\left(2x + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -1$
$\cos\left(2x + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
Let $u = 2x + \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, where $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \le u \le \dfrac{17\pi}{4}$.
$\cos u = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
Reference angle: $u_{\text{ref}} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$
In $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{17\pi}{4}\right]$: $u = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}, \dfrac{8\pi}{3}, \dfrac{10\pi}{3}$
Subtract $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$2x = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}, \dfrac{13\pi}{12}, \dfrac{29\pi}{12}, \dfrac{37\pi}{12}$
Divide by 2:
$x = \dfrac{5\pi}{24}, \dfrac{13\pi}{24}, \dfrac{29\pi}{24}, \dfrac{37\pi}{24}$
